name: City Drift
description: A networked multiplayer racer where players build the track before they race it. I built the track editor: anchor-based snapping, overlap detection, and other functionality.

contributions.title: Track editor
contributions.body: Designed and built TrackBuilder (485 of its 511 lines), including the piece palette, anchor snapping, and flip controls.

contributions.title: Overlap detection
contributions.body: Used layer masks with an inflation margin so pieces that merely touch aren't rejected as overlapping.

key_features.title: Player-built tracks
key_features.body: Tracks are serialized and sent over the network so both players race the same layout.

key_features.title: Build timer
key_features.body: A 60-second limit keeps the pre-race phase moving.

name: How AI is Reshaping the Job Market
description: A scroll-driven narrative about how AI is changing employment, where the charts advance as you read rather than sitting still beside the text. I wrote 4,076 of the 4,951 lines of JavaScript in the published build, including the layer that maps reading position to the active visualization, both choropleth maps, and the job-vulnerability views.

contributions.title: Narrative orchestration
contributions.body: Wrote scroll-narrative.js, 321 of its 350 lines, which decides which visualization is active at a given scroll position and drives the transition into the next one. It sits on top of the third-party scroll-watcher library rather than replacing it.

contributions.title: Choropleth maps
contributions.body: Built the United States and world maps end to end, 414 and 353 lines, both entirely mine, sharing one interaction model so state-level and country-level patterns read the same way.

contributions.title: Job vulnerability views
contributions.body: Wrote the combined view, the animated transition between encodings, the scatter, and the scroll variant, roughly 1,390 lines across four files.

contributions.title: Opportunity and skill demand
contributions.body: Wrote high-ai-opportunity-scroll.js at 874 lines and skill-demand-changes-scroll.js at 456 lines, both entirely mine, plus the light and dark theming.

contributions.title: Exploratory analysis
contributions.body: Five Python notebooks covering preprocessing, state-level analysis, and threat scoring, which determined what the final views would actually show.

key_features.title: Charts driven by reading position
key_features.body: Each section advances the visualization instead of swapping it out, so the argument and the data move together rather than competing for attention.

key_features.title: Two-column layout
key_features.body: Visualizations hold the left three quarters of the screen while the text column updates alongside, so a chart stays in view while you read about it.

key_features.title: Animated transitions between encodings
key_features.body: Charts morph rather than cut when the question changes, which keeps the reader oriented instead of forcing them to re-read the axes.

key_features.title: Process book
key_features.body: The published write-up covers the sketches, the data decisions, and the revisions made after user testing.

client: Data Visualization final project, team of 4

name: Course Page: Design & Implementation
description: A custom-built, responsive landing page for an enterprise-level workforce learning initiative, course page utilizing Thought Industries' Custom Code panel. The page serves as an entry portal for users to learn about, explore, and begin a microcredential program designed to bridge engineering competition skills with professional career readiness.

contributions.title: Frontend Development
contributions.body: Coded the layout completely from scratch using HTML and CSS directly within the Thought Industries platform code editor, ensuring responsive design principles and custom styling aligned with strict enterprise branding guidelines.

contributions.title: Asset Management & Infrastructure
contributions.body: Architected and configured the file storage systems required to host, manage, and deliver the page's digital assets (images, badges, and icons) efficiently.

key_features.title: Hero Section
key_features.body: Highlights the program's value proposition ('Expedite'), outlines key skills gained (such as Collaboration, Product Lifecycle Management, and Digital Engineering), and displays a custom digital achievement badge alongside practical course metrics (Difficulty Level and Time Commitment).

key_features.title: The Learning Roadmap
key_features.body: A clean, structured multi-column section featuring curated imagery and descriptive summaries for three foundational courses tracking a user's journey from competition basics to launching their career.

key_features.title: Benefits & Value Proposition
key_features.body: A dedicated footer section detailing the importance of continuous upskilling and professional marketability.

name: Digital Badging Application Redesign
description: A global engineering software company issues academic credentials to computer-aided design learners worldwide, and the application that manages them had grown to 24 pages without anyone stepping back to look at it as a whole. People got lost in it. I led the full interface overhaul, work originally scoped for a team of five developers, restructuring the navigation around what people were actually trying to do and grounding every decision in research rather than taste.

contributions.title: Led the overhaul alone
contributions.body: Redesigned all 24 pages of the internal badging application, work originally scoped for a five-developer team, from research through high-fidelity prototypes.

contributions.title: Ran the research
contributions.body: Conducted a dozen stakeholder interviews and Wizard of Oz usability tests, where a person plays the role of the system so a flow can be tested before it is built.

contributions.title: Synthesized findings with rainbow sheets
contributions.body: A spreadsheet that lines up every participant's observations side by side, so patterns surface across sessions instead of resting on the loudest interview.

contributions.title: Built the prototypes
contributions.body: Produced high-fidelity Figma prototypes and custom Photoshop assets for the interface and its supporting documentation.

contributions.title: Administered the programs behind it
contributions.body: Managed 300+ global credentialing programs serving over 10,000 computer-aided design learners, which is how I learned where the system actually broke down.

key_features.title: Navigation rebuilt around tasks
key_features.body: The original 24 pages were grouped by internal structure rather than by what people came to do. Regrouping them cut the number of places a user had to look.

key_features.title: Wayfinding and signage
key_features.body: Clearer labels and consistent positional cues so users could tell where they were in the system and what came next.

key_features.title: Reduced cognitive load
key_features.body: Fewer competing elements per screen, so the primary action on each page is the obvious one.

key_features.title: Research-led iteration
key_features.body: Each round of changes traced back to a specific observed failure, not a preference.
